newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss legislator urges freezing of Mobutu accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss legislator urges freezing of Mobutu accounts.

text.p: A Swiss member of parliament urged the government and banks on Wednesday to freeze billions of dollars Zaire's embattled ruler Mobutu Sese Seko may have deposited in Switzerland.
The appeal from social democrat deputy Remo Gysin and a Berne-based activist group echoed an earlier call by Zaire's rebel leader, Laurent Kabila, for the return of Mobutu's fortunes.

"Dictator Mobutu is well known to have greatly enriched himself at the cost of the Zairean people," said a statement from Gysin and the group Action on Swiss-Third World Finances, where Gysin is board member.

"At least part of his (Mobutu's) billions in wealth are presumably deposited or invested in the financial centre Switzerland...For this reason the Swiss government, banks and asset managers are called on to act quickly," it said.
A spokeswoman for the Swiss Bankers Association said banks saw no need to take special action at this stage.
"We assume that the banks are aware of their responsibility. They also follow what is happening in the world. There is no need to call for extra vigilence," she told Reuters.
It was not even clear Mobutu had money in Swiss banks, she added.
"As far as banks are concerned, we are not aware of any reasons to believe that this is so," she said.
The 66-year-old Zairean ruler has prostate cancer and has been in Europe during much of the rebellion in the east since undergoing surgery in Switzerland last August.
Mobutu's holdings in Switzerland are widely estimated by Swiss media at around $4 billion, a number Gysin said was based on a statement by Zaire's finance minister in 1982.
"If you add the interest over time, you come up with over $8 billion today," he said. Gysin's Social Democrats are one of four parties in the centre-right Swiss government coalition.
Kabila, whose fighters control much of the east of Zaire, urged Switzerland last month to hand back Mobutu's wealth in a German radio interview, saying the money was stolen from the people of Zaire.

Gysin told Reuters his group wanted the government and banks to at least consider freezing any Mobutu accounts or other assets to prevent them from being quietly moved for concealment in more secretive places than Switzerland.
Switzerland has been the scene of legal battles over bank accounts of fallen leaders including the late Philippine ruler Ferdinand Marcos and Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier.

"I think the banks have learned something since Marcos's time," the bankers association spokeswoman said. "Dictators have also learned something. Our banking system is safe for customers who are not criminals, but a bad place to hide criminal money."
Gysin saw parallels between the cases of Mobutu and Marcos, whose accounts in Swiss banks were blocked by Berne government with an emergency decree in 1986 after he was ousted.

"I could imagine that an emergency decree could be used in the case of Mobutu to freeze his assets. I think the Federal Council (cabinet) should be considering this and I think it would be an obvious step," he said.
The Swiss foreign ministry, asked about the usual procedure for similar cases, declined to comment.
